description: Our six-member team combines experience in competitive programming, mathematics olympiads, AI, scientific research, and startup development. We have developed AI-powered apps, participated in national and international hackathons, and won startup competitions. Our projects include Signova, OpportuNet, NeuroBelt, and PheroCrop. We bring complementary skills in software development, data analysis, machine learning, hardware, and engineering, enabling us to build practical, innovative solutions.
summary: SkyBlink turns NASA’s new SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey into a tool anyone can use to spot things that move, flicker or look strange. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours every six months, but so much data arrives that most changes are never looked at. Our Python engine does the heavy work automatically. It finds faint moving objects that are invisible in every single exposure: it “shift-and-stacks” hundreds of images along possible motions, then rejects artifacts with automatic checks and injection–recovery tests. It compares WISE 2010 with SPHEREx 2026 to catch nearby stars crawling across the sky. It averages whole survey passes to detect real brightness changes. And it combines SPHEREx’s six detectors to flag unusually red objects such as cold brown dwarfs. A static website then presents the results as four “lenses” (Fast movers, Slow movers, Blinking stars, Strange colours), with Gaia and WISE overlays, a live Aladin sky map, and a review button so people can mark each candidate “real” or “artifact”. Software finds the candidates; humans make the final call.
details:
What it does. SkyBlink is a pipeline plus a website. The pipeline (Python, Google Colab) queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for every SPHEREx exposure of a field, downloads cutouts, aligns them on one sky grid, and runs four analyses (“lenses”):

Fast movers (hidden movers): shift-and-stack over a grid of velocities, so an object too faint to see in any single exposure adds up into a clear point. Each detection is checked automatically: distance to bright-star residuals, image edges, a signal in both halves of the observations, and significance above an empirical noise threshold. Injection–recovery tests with artificial objects measure what the pipeline can really find. Because each SPHEREx detector sees a different wavelength, every track also gets a 6-colour spectrum, used to guess what the object is (asteroid-like vs brown-dwarf-like).
Slow movers (time machine): blinks AllWISE 2010 images against SPHEREx 2026 in matching bands. Our measured motions agree with catalogue proper motions: Barnard’s Star 167.4″ (expected 167.7″), WISE 0855 132.8″ (129.5″), Epsilon Indi B 75.2″ (74.4″).
Blinking stars: compares survey-pass averages against nearby comparison stars, so SPHEREx’s changing wavelength cannot fake variability. Example: RW Aurigae varies about 21× more than steady stars in the same field.
Strange colours: per-detector stacks from blue (0.93 µm) to red (4.7 µm) rank how red each source is. Example: Epsilon Indi B shows the methane dip near 3.3 µm typical of cold brown dwarfs; RW Aurigae is very red because of warm dust, not because it is cold, and the site explains that difference.
(Add only if the spectrum run succeeds:) Full spectrum: for a chosen star we measure every exposure at its exact wavelength from SPHEREx’s spectral WCS, giving a ~100-point spectrum instead of 6 colours.

Website. Static HTML/CSS/JavaScript hosted on GitHub Pages, with no server and no account needed. For each target you flip through frames, use the difference view, choose the field of view, and see per-frame metadata. The Aladin Lite sky map overlays Gaia DR3 stars and WISE, 2MASS or DSS backgrounds. Every candidate has a review panel (“Real object / Artifact / I found something”), and reviews can be exported as JSON or CSV. Search accepts star names (resolved with CDS Sesame) or coordinates, and coordinates can be passed in the URL so the tool can be linked or embedded elsewhere.

Easy to update. Adding a target or a new SPHEREx data release means adding one line to the engine’s target list and re-running the notebook. Results are written as small JSON and PNG files that the site loads automatically.

Honesty by design. The demo objects are planted on purpose and labelled “artificial test object”. The site never calls a candidate a discovery. Marginal candidates are shown as candidates, and the “Artifact” button exists exactly for them.

Tools: Python, Astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, Google Colab, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Aladin Lite, GitHub Pages, Render.

Impact. SPHEREx data arrive every week. SkyBlink shows that software can pre-sort that flood into a short, explained list of candidates, so students and citizen scientists spend their time judging real possibilities instead of scanning empty images. It is also a teaching tool for how astronomers find nearby stars, brown dwarfs, and variable stars.
